The only things I think are immoral are things that cause suffering for beings that doesn't deserve it. Can include anything from being needlessly mean to someone fragile to murder to corporation-scale pollution.

I think it's useful to make a distinction between morals and ethics. (People have different opinions as to what these words mean, and my definition is not necessarily the correct or even the most common one).

In my view, ethics refers to the rules governing a role, whereas morality refers to the rules governing yourself. For example, if I'm a school teacher or a doctor, that role imposes certain rules - ethics - that I have to follow in certain situations. I might be compelled to take a baggie of weed from a student or compelled to keep a patient's secret, even if it disagrees with my personal feelings.

My morality, on the other hand, belongs only to me.

I am not religious so I see morality as subjective. Others believe in a universal right and wrong even if they struggle to define it in detail. I take a pretty hardcore view of the implications of subjective morality, essentially dispensing with the concepts of right or wrong entirely, and replacing them with simple preferences.

What's right to me is that which genuinely feels right, and it can change over time. I believe that this is the bottom line for most people, even if they would never express it that way themselves.

Verisimilitude. They can either take control away for a split second while you interact with certain items, or you can watch that lever or button flip/push itself.

As far as the the QT moments in that game, they are very brief and barely noticeable. I would hardly call it "briefly taking control away from the player" so much as I would call it "briefly and explicitly illustrating a task that cannot be replicated properly in a control scheme". I think it is just a little bit of polish so that when you activate a lever it doesn't "magically" move, etc.

Everyone complains about the QT executions in that game, and normally I am inclined to agree for most games, but in this case they are actually kind of fun, very short, quite varied, and have important and skill-based gameplay elements in mind with their design (you build health and armor with executions). You can modify the way the executions work in a variety of ways, including making them quicker (and then even quicker), making it so you can do them from further away, making them easier to perform, etc. I think there are obviously ways to improve them or maybe even replace them, but overall they are not poorly implemented or shoehorned in imo, so I don't see what all the fuss is about. I thought they added a little something extra to how you play the game, namely getting your ass into the fray. They are a bit "too necessary" if I had to make a critical judgement. I get the criticism, and welcome it actually, but I personally think it is way overblown in this case.
